ei.title: Chapter 3-08: The Quest for Certainty in Knowledge
ei.subject: 올림포스독해의기본1

fullPassage: Knowledge, for science, aims to be proven knowledge, justified by evidence and reason. Nothing is accepted as true unless it has been proved to be so, or there are good reasons to believe that it will be at some point in the future. This reflects the philosophical quest for certainty that goes back to René Descartes, who refused to accept anything that he could not know for certain to be true. He hoped to base all knowledge on self-evident propositions, and thought that reason should take priority over observation. Descartes was aware that his senses frequently misled him. The implication of this — a view which had a long history, prior to the rise of science — was that, if the evidence of our senses did not conform to reason, it was likely that they were in error.
